subject: stacked-data single-season vs. multi-season models: is the former good enough when the latter is possible?

messages.author: d3fd439c2e48caf1
messages.subject: stacked-data single-season vs. multi-season models: is the former good enough when the latter is possible?
parts:
Greetings unmarked community,

I recently reviewed a manuscript that had clear value and represented an important contribution (I'll go light on the details for obvious reasons of confidentiality) that employed a stacked single-season abundance (N-mixture) model (via pcount) for an animal population data set with repeated within-year counts over several decades. One focus of the manuscript was on estimating (exponential) population growth rates under a variety of scenarios. To estimate growth rates, a site covariate (year) was added to model abundance, much as is commonly done in a mixed-effects Poisson or negative binomial GLM when detection is assumed (explicitly or otherwise) to be 1. There was no clear rationale for using pcount (vs. the Dail-Madsen [via pcountOpen]) model in this paper (beyond addressing detection) and there was nothing to indicated systematic issues in the data (i.e., entire years missing) required the use of a stacked single-season model. 

Perhaps I'm a little too attached to open-population models as implemented in unmarked (I've published three papers using these models), but it struck me as non-trivially problematic that the authors chose to use the stacked single-season model, particularly since pcountOpen offers the "trend" dynamic to estimate growth rates from sequential years (N[i,t] = N[i,t-1]*gamma). In my understanding, this estimation of gamma (trend/growth) from year-to-year site-level changes in abundance (when data allows it) is far more robust than estimation via a year covariate in a stacked-data single-season model. I tried to state my concerns as clearly and constructively as possible and the AE is requiring the authors to respond to my concerns. However, the overall assessment by the AE (and, in turn, the ME) was that my concerns did not warrant a revision to the analysis.

I certainly don't want to "sink" a valuable analysis (not that it appears I could even if I wanted to), I'm just of the strong opinion that using multi-season models are the right tool for the job (here pcountOpen rather than pcount) when there appears no necessity to using a stacked-data model. To be clear, I don't in any way think stacked-data single-season models are "wrong" (as has been discussed and revisited; https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/unmarked/OHkk98y09Zo/6gRiEowXNeMJ), but in this case I believe there is a clear "right" way to proceed when revising this analysis (at least in a MLE framework =)).

What do you all think? Are my concerns warranted or do I just sound like an angry old man shouting at kids on my lawn? I welcome any on- or off-list responses and will try to respond with extreme care to any on-list questions.

Grateful for the unmarked community and the package developers, as always.

- Giancarlo

messages.author: 4a635fe980c8c1cd
messages.subject: stacked-data single-season vs. multi-season models: is the former good enough when the latter is possible?
parts:
Spitballing, but the exponential growth model fit by ‘trend’ is a little different than a stacked model with a log-linear trend for E(N)—one sometimes problematic property of the former is that if N_i ever hits 0, it gets stuck w/out modeling a rescue. Maybe also if annual increases in abundance are more random spatially vs. accumulating faster in sites where N was previously larger, the stacked model makes a little more sense?

John

messages.author: d3fd439c2e48caf1
messages.subject: Re: stacked-data single-season vs. multi-season models: is the former good enough when the latter is possible?
parts: Thanks John, that's a condition I hadn't considered. I'm remembering now that I dealt with this in the past by adding an immigration parameter with covariates (how easy to forget this stuff). I don't think the stuck-at-zero issue motivated the authors' choice to assume spatially random population growth, but I think this assumption could be supported with adequate citation. Thanks again.  - Giancarlo

messages.subject: Re: stacked-data single-season vs. multi-season models: is the former good enough when the latter is possible?
parts: Just thinking about this a little more, it probably makes sense as a general practice to do some additional model-checking when stacking beyond the omnibus g-o-f tests (eg., looking for serial correlation in residuals by site or whatever), but I’m not really familiar with any specific tests.

messages.subject: Re: stacked-data single-season vs. multi-season models: is the former good enough when the latter is possible?
parts:
I think that's a great suggestion, John. I'll see what I can come up with, perhaps using Durbin-Watson on site-year residuals ... but what a site-year residual is in the context of pcount/pcountOpen is a little murky in my mind (perhaps via some augmentation of the Moore and Swihart approach to site- or site-year occupancy residuals...?).

I thought this stacked vs. non-stacked question might generate a little more discussion, but I recognize (1) it's summer and (2) my posts can give some folks a case of the TL;DRs.  - G
